title: Token cost grid for mixed arrival workloads (draft)
body:
Purpose:
This working note lays out a compact spreadsheet-driven framework (token-cost grid) for evaluating continuous-batching + concurrency sizing across mixed arrival patterns. Objective is pragmatic: produce a small set of default knob recommendations that minimize $/token at target p95 latency bands (50ms, 100ms, 250ms) while exposing the tradeoffs for tail-heavy vs bursty workloads.

Context / Why this is different:
- Existing docs have explored batch windows and elasticity separately; this draft focuses on 'mixed arrivals' (concurrent steady stream + intermittent microbursts) and visualizing a 2D cost surface: concurrency x batch-window.
- Intention is a shareable spreadsheet that SRE, product, and cost-ops can use to pick operating points and sanity-check Dedicated sizing.

Assumptions (explicit):
- Model cost baseline: pGPU cost normalized to tokens/sec-of-GPU; use local calibration table from infra/pricebench (ref linked_artifacts).
- Two request classes: steady (lambda_s) and burst (lambda_b) with Poisson arrivals for steady and short-duration elevated rate for bursts.
- Average prompt length = 32 tokens; average generation length = 64 tokens (configurable knobs in spreadsheet).
- KV cache hit rate ignored for first pass (we add a cache factor later).
- Scheduling: continuous-batching engine collects requests into an active window T_w (ms) then issues inference when either concurrency hits C_max or T_w expires.
- Concurrency C is defined as simultaneous in-flight model invocations on a single worker. Multiprocessing and multi-GPU treated as linear aggregate capacity.
- Target SLOs evaluated at p95 response time measured at request ingress (includes queue delay + service time).

Spreadsheet layout (tabs):
1) params: knobs (lambda_s, burst profile: amp & duration, prompt/generation tokens, model throughput/tokens-per-second at given batch sizes, overhead per request)
2) service-curve: measured latencies for single-invocation vs batch size (empirical numbers) and kernel scaling row (for quick interpolation)
3) simulator: discrete-event simplified sim that approximates queueing + batch dispatch; outputs p50/p95/p99 and avg cost/token per scenario; implemented as spreadsheet formulas (no macros)
4) grid: condensed table where rows = concurrency choices (1,2,4,8,16,32), columns = window (1ms,5ms,10ms,25ms,50ms,100ms). Cells show p95 (color-coded) and $$ per token (sortable text)
5) recommendations: auto-suggest operating points by SLO band and cost bracket

Key knobs and heuristics captured in the sheet:
- Effective batch efficiency curve: latency_per_token(batch) = kernel_latency(batch)/batch + per_request_overhead
- Small-window penalty: when T_w is tiny relative to inter-arrival, batching collapses -> cost up, but latency low; capture threshold where average batch size >= 2 is cost-effective
- Concurrency smoothing: Increasing C reduces queueing but increases per-token marginal cost due to resource reservation; include a utilization curve mapping concurrency->idle fraction
- Burst absorbency: measure how long a burst takes to evacuate for a given (C, T_w) pair; if evacuation > burst duration, SLO breach occurs for subsequent requests

Representative numbers (example scenario - replace with measured numbers):
- model throughput single token: 120k tokens/s (on test GPU) at batch=1; at batch=8 throughput per token improves by ~1.8x; at batch=32 improvements plateau at 2.1x
- overhead per request (RPC + decode loop): 0.8ms
- steady lambda_s: 8 req/s; burst: 320 req/s for 2s every 60s

Simulation summary (quick pass):
- Low-latency band (p95 <= 50ms): best cost points tend to be C=1..4 with T_w <= 5ms. Cost/token is high (baseline x1.9) because batching opportunity limited. Bursts cause transient SLO spikes unless we allow a short spillover concurrency increase or fallback model with lower latency.
- Mid band (p95 <= 100ms): sweet spot often at C=4..8 and T_w=10..25ms; average batch size >= 6 during steady periods, bursts are absorbed without large queue growth in most trials. Cost/token ~ baseline x1.1-1.3.
- Relaxed band (p95 <= 250ms): C=8..32 with T_w=25..100ms gives the best cost/token (~baseline x0.75–0.9) but risk of persistent queue if bursts are very long.

Example grid excerpt (textual):
- C=2, T_w=5ms -> p95 62ms, cost/token = $0.000014 (higher during bursts)
- C=8, T_w=25ms -> p95 112ms, cost/token = $0.000009 (better amortized)
- C=16, T_w=100ms -> p95 210ms, cost/token = $0.000006 (best unit cost but high tail risk)

Recommendations (initial):
- Default profiles to publish in console: "latency:low" (p95<=50ms), "latency:balanced" (p95<=100ms), "latency:cost-optimized" (p95<=250ms). Each mapping to a suggested (C_min, T_w) and an autoscaler policy: allow C to scale +2 for 5s on burst detection, then decay 30s.
- For mixed-arrival customers, enable prefix-cache-first heuristics (cheap cache hits reduce generation tokens and shift optima left).
- Add a safeguard: when observed instantaneous QPS > 4x steady, switch to a fast-fallback model (smaller, lower latency) until backlog drained.

Open questions / TODOs:
- Inject measured kernel-level throughput numbers for the most common models (gpt-medium, gpt-large analogs). Current numbers are synthetic; need bench runs on dedicated clusters (ticket INF-4821).
- Add KV/prefix cache model factor and rerun grid; cache reduces marginal cost dramatically for many customer workloads.
- Validate spreadsheet sim against the production tracing dataset for 3 customers (extracts in linked_artifacts).
- Define comfort thresholds for autoscaler scale-up magnitude during microbursts (safe default: +50% concurrency, bounded by reserved capacity).

Action plan / experiments to run next 2 weeks:
1) Run microbench sweep for batch sizes [1,2,4,8,16,32] for top 3 model types on staging-GPU (owners: Elena/Noah). Timeline: 3 days.
2) Replace synthetic throughput/latency rows in sheet and re-generate grids for 10 realistic arrival mixes (owner: Maya). Timeline: 2 days.
3) Run a 24h trace-replay for customer-A (bursty chat app) and compare spreadsheet p95 predictions vs actual; iterate model. Timeline: 5 days (Ravi).
4) Draft recommend profiles and add to Console reclaim page (PR to product-docs). Timeline: 3 days.

Notes / scratch thoughts (quick):
- Consider exposing "burst absorbency" metric in console: seconds-to-evict-90pct-of-current-backlog at current C/T_w
- Where possible expose both cost/token and cost/second curves to help capacity decisions (some teams care about $/day burn as well as unit cost)
- For Dedicated customers, translate token-cost grid to reserved-GPU counts with headroom buffer = max(20% or burst-quantile)

Appendix (spreadsheet formulas / hints):
- approximate p95 latency = quantile(queue_distribution + service_time, 0.95) where queue_distribution approximated by M/G/C with batching conversion; spreadsheet uses an empirical adjustment factor when utilization>0.7 to account for large-tail effects.
- cost/token = (GPU_hourly_cost * active_hours_per_day + amortized_overheads) / total_tokens_served_in_period; derive tokens_served from simulated throughput * duration

Contact / owners: Maya Chen (primary), Ravi Patel (sim validation), Elena Smirnova (benchmarks), Noah Brooks (infra perf traces).

If you use this sheet: save a copy, name it like "token-cost-grid-<cust>-YYYYMMDD" and add a short note in the Recommendations tab with observed trajectory.

End of draft.
summary: Draft design for a spreadsheet-based token-cost grid to evaluate cost vs latency tradeoffs for continuous-batching + concurrency sizing under mixed arrival patterns. Contains assumptions, spreadsheet layout, preliminary sim results, recommended default profiles, open questions, and a short experimental plan.
